Revilings
re-vi'lingz
n. pl. (contemptuous or abusive speech; reproaches)
From revile, Old French reviler, to hold cheap, from re- and vil, vile — literally to make vile, to treat a man as worthless by speech.

Biblical Definition

Revilings are words used as weapons, and the Authorized Version records God's attention to them twice. The first is a command to a persecuted remnant: “Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings” (Isa 51:7). The people addressed are marked by the law being in the heart, and what they are told is not to answer, argue, or out-shout, but not to be afraid. The second shows why: “I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border” (Zep 2:8). God has been listening the whole time, and the reviling of His people is filed as an offence against Him. The Christian's pattern is his Lord: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1Pe 2:23). And the reviled are pronounced blessed rather than pitied: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reviling as reproaching; treating with opprobrious language; and as a noun, the act of vilifying, reproachful language.

expand to see more

REVI'LING, ppr. Reproaching; treating with opprobrious or contemptuous language.

REVI'LING, n. The act of vilifying; reproachful language; contemptuous speech.

Neither be ye afraid of their revilings. Isa. 51.

To revile is from re and vile; that is, to make vile, to treat as worthless.

Revilers are ranked in Scripture with the covetous and the extortioners. 1 Cor. 6.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 51:7 — "Hearken unto me, ye that know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings."

Zephaniah 2:8 — "I have heard the reproach of Moab, and the revilings of the children of Ammon, whereby they have reproached my people, and magnified themselves against their border."

1 Peter 2:23 — "Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:"

Matthew 5:11 — "Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake."

Modern Corruption

Reviling has been industrialized by the network age, and the church has largely joined in rather than absorbed it.

expand to see more

Every age has revilers; this one has given them a distribution system, a scoreboard, and an income. The machinery rewards contempt because contempt performs, and the result is a public square in which making another man vile is a career. Isaiah 51:7 speaks directly to those under it and says a surprising thing: not answer them but fear them not. The fear is the real damage. A church that is afraid of revilings will trim its preaching long before anyone lays a hand on it, which is why the command is addressed precisely to the people who have the law in their heart.

The graver failure is the church reviling back. 1 Peter 2:23 records that Christ, who had every fact on His side and infinite power in reserve, reviled not again — and the reason given is not that He was above it but that He committed himself to him that judgeth righteously. Non-retaliation is an act of faith in a real coming judgment, not a strategy of niceness. Where that judgment is doubted, believers take their own case in hand and answer contempt with contempt. 1 Peter 3:9 forbids it plainly: not railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gidduph (H1421), reviling, reproach; Greek loidoreo (G3058), to revile, to abuse; Old French reviler, to make vile.

expand to see more

Hebrew gidduphotam (H1421) — their revilings, blasphemies; Isaiah 51:7, and the same root is used of blasphemy against God.

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, scorn; paired with revilings in both Isaiah 51:7 and Zephaniah 2:8.

Greek loidoroumenos ouk anteloidorei (G3058) — being reviled, He reviled not in return; 1 Peter 2:23.

Greek oneidisosin (G3679) — they shall reproach; Matthew 5:11, where the reviled are called blessed.

Old French reviler, from vil — to make vile; the etymology names the intent exactly.

Usage

"“Neither be ye afraid of their revilings” — not answer them; fear them not."

"“I have heard the reproach of Moab” — He has been listening the whole time."

"“Reviled not again… but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” — restraint resting on a real judgment."
